newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish cabinet adopts key bill on pension funds.
newsitem.headline: Polish cabinet adopts key bill on pension funds.

text.p: Poland's cabinet on Tuesday adopted a draft law on pension funds, a key plank of its vital social security reform, the minister steering the changes said.

"The government adopted the draft of the law on pension funds, which will form the basis for the second pillar of the new social security system in Poland," Jerzy Hausner told reporters after a cabinet meeting.
He said the bill would go before parliament next week.
Hausner, government plenipotentiary for the reform, said the draft provided safeguards to guarantee the safety of contributions, so the new funds would enjoy public confidence.
"These must be financial institutions about which people are totally convinced that they are absolutely safe," he said.

In Poland's present creaking hand-to-mouth system left from the communist era, employers pass the state Social Insurance Office (ZUS) contributions totalling 45 percent of their workers' gross pay and ZUS pays pensioners from current income.
Despite the bloated contributions, ZUS, the sole pensions provider, still needs subsidies from the central budget which now account for 15 percent of budget spending.
Poland's ageing population threatens the collapse of the system in the next decade if nothing is done soon.
Under the government's reform part of pensions will still be paid to pensioners as now but some contributions will be put in the new pension funds which will invest the money.
The so-called third pillar will involve voluntary payments to fully private pension schemes for those who choose.
Hausner said the bill did not specify what proportion of the compulsory employers' contributions will be tranferred to the pension funds nor how quickly.
"We are not anticipating now what proportion of the contributions (to ZUS) will be carried across, by whom, and therefore at what rate and to what extent the reform will be carried out," he said.

Hausner said the funds would be run by private pension companies, which will be legally obliged to ensure an appropriate rate of return on the investments and will be allowed to go bankrupt if they functioned badly.
"A fund cannot go under, but the firm managing it can, and in such a case we forsee mechanisms for transferring the fund's contributions to a different management company," Hausner said.
"The funds will be able to invest in Polish and foreign securities, especially in government paper, but under very clearly defined conditions," he said.
He said the funds and managers would be policed by and Supervision Office for Pension Funds (UNFE) under a president appointed by the prime minister.
The government anticipates that 10 to 12 pension funds will be created but their number will be decided by the UNFE chief.
He said that the bill called for appointment of a banking deposit holder to be entrusted with the funds' assets.

Last week the government approved a bill on issuing convertible bonds, exchangeable for shares of privatised firms, to finance the reform, principles of which were this week approved by a committee grouping trade unions and employers.

The government hopes these two bills and a third, on social insurance in industrial sectors, should be approved before parliament's summer vacation, so the reform can take effect by the target date of January 1, 1999. -- Warsaw Newsroom +48 22 653 9700
